'''Elizabeth "Betty" Johnson''' '''PhD''' (18 October 1936 – 11 September 2003) was an American [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] with a PhD in elementary particle theory, who was awarded an MBE in 2002 for "services to people returning to careers in science, engineering and technology". Johnson was influential in establishing the [[Daphne Jackson Trust]] and was one of the first women to receive a fellowship after a career break for family commitments. Johnson died after a long fight with breast cancer on September 11th, 2003. 

== Career and research ==
Johnson was born in [[Philadelphia]]. She received a BA in physics and mathematics at [[Swarthmore College]], Pennsylvania in 1958.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=MacKinnon|first=Angus|last2=Pendry|first2=John|date=2004-04-01|title=Elizabeth Ann Johnson|journal=Physics Today|volume=57|issue=4|pages=105–106|doi=10.1063/1.1752438|issn=0031-9228|bibcode=2004PhT....57d.105M|doi-access=free}}</ref> She completed a PhD in elementary particle physics at the [[University of Manchester]] with support of the State Department [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright Scholarship]] scheme between 1958 – 1960, and an honorary [[Woodrow Wilson National Fellowship Foundation|Woodrow Wilson fellow]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2003/oct/09/guardianobituaries.highereducation|title=Obituary: Betty Johnson|last=Perry|first=Katie|date=2003-10-09|work=The Guardian|access-date=2017-11-02|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> She continued her research in the [[University of Pittsburgh]], [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], [[King's College London]] and the [[University of Auckland]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2003|title=Betty Johnson: 1936–2003|journal=Physics World|language=en|volume=16|issue=11|pages=11|doi=10.1088/2058-7058/16/11/19|issn=2058-7058}}</ref> Johnson held several part-time positions at the [[University of Surrey]] whilst raising two children. In 1975 Johnson was elected a fellow of the [[Institute of Physics]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/policy/diversity/initiatives/lecture/page_42787.html|title=Elizabeth Johnson Memorial Lecture|last=Physics|first=Institute of|website=www.iop.org|language=en-GB|access-date=2017-11-02}}</ref>

Her research interests evolved from [[elementary particle theory]] to [[gas dynamics]] and spin-dependent effects in [[semiconductor]]s. Her work focused on understanding [[fundamental physics]] and using it to predict the properties of real materials.<ref name=":0" />

During her time at the [[University of Surrey]], Johnson became a colleague and friend of [[Daphne Jackson]], the first woman in the United Kingdom to become a professor of physics.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/article/lives-in-brief-hvfh2l9lc7l|title=Lives in Brief|date=2003-10-08|work=[[The Times]]|access-date=2017-11-02|issn=0140-0460}}</ref> When Daphne Jackson began to award fellowships for women who wanted to resume research after taking a break from their careers; Johnson was one of the first recipients. In 1986 Johnson joined the Condensed Matter Theory Group at [[Imperial College London]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/college.asp?P=3517|title=Reporter – In brief|website=www.imperial.ac.uk|access-date=2017-11-02}}</ref>

Johnson was crucial in establishing the [[Daphne Jackson Trust]] after Jackson's death in 1992. She became a trustee in 2002, as well as sitting on the council of the [[Women's Engineering Society]].<ref name=":1" /> She was awarded in an [[Order of the British Empire|MBE]] for her commitment to women in science in 2002.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/in_depth/uk/2002/birthday_honours_2002/2045233.stm|title=MBEs: I – M|date=2002-06-14|access-date=2017-11-02|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref name=":1" />
